paragraphs: President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russia sanctions is meant to keep Moscow at the negotiating table, according to the BBC. In a Truth Social post he said he is "in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine" and did not want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." He also said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."

The BBC reported that Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Friday night, two days before they were due to take effect. Congress passed the measures and Trump signed them into law in September. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the move as a 60-day pause to analyse the potential effect on the US and global economies. The Washington Examiner reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also called it a 60-day period "so we can examine what's going on" and said on Sunday that "the only thing that has been lifted is the diesel embargo." The Examiner described the executive order as waiving sweeping sanctions and tariffs, which sits uneasily with Bessent's narrower description.

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev called the order "an important and truly historic moment" and said the sanctions would have caused "serious damage" to the US and global markets. Zelensky told NBC News that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake". He said he believed the administration would lift more sanctions. He has repeatedly said Putin does not want peace.

The BBC said relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine and its European allies criticised that plan, and Zelensky said it amounted to the US investing in Russia's war effort. Zelensky has also raised concerns about Starlink disruption and intelligence sharing; Trump has denied both. The 60-day review period is the next marker to watch.

Kenya has confirmed an eighth Ebola case, according to Al Jazeera. Health Director-General Patrick Amoth told Citizen TV that of 38 people tested on Sunday, one returned a positive result. He described the patient as a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker and who developed fever, headache and muscle pain.

Amoth said the man worked as a patient attendant, cleaning utensils and linens, and was likely exposed to Kenya's first Ebola case, discovered earlier this month. A Ministry of Health source said he developed symptoms on Saturday, was quarantined and was then tested. The first patient had travelled from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to Nairobi and died at a Nairobi hospital on October 5. On Saturday the ministry reported four new cases, three of them health workers who treated that patient. The ministry said the fourth was a relative of the deceased man.

The outbreak is of the Bundibugyo strain, for which Al Jazeera says there is no vaccine or specific treatment. In the DRC, where it began in May, at least 9,400 cases have been recorded, including more than 4,500 deaths, in what the outlet calls the country's deadliest outbreak. Ituri province in the east remains the epicentre, with almost three quarters of confirmed cases according to government data. The government announced Sunday that the virus has reached an eighth province, North Ubangi.

State news agency ACP reported that North Kivu, where the World Health Organization says substantial transmission continues, will ban people entering from Ituri for one week from Monday. Planned measures also include limits on passengers in cars and on motorbikes and a suspension of large public gatherings. Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases and two deaths before being declared Ebola-free in August.

Pope Leo XIV thanked about 15,000 people gathered in St Peter's Square on Sunday in his first major public appearance since lung cancer surgery, Al Jazeera reported. Speaking from a window overlooking the square during the traditional Angelus blessing, he said: "Now that this delicate phase is behind me, I will gradually resume my activities, always with God's help and your prayers."

The 71-year-old pope had revealed a week earlier, at the same blessing, that a nodule had been found in his lung and would be removed. The operation confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. Test results to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending. Leo said the past week had made him feel especially close to those facing illness, and he expressed particular gratitude to the doctors, nurses and staff at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, where he was treated. After pausing and waving, he returned to his apartment in the Apostolic Palace.

People in the crowd welcomed his return. A delegation from Africa, in Rome for a Catholic meeting, danced and ululated after the blessing. Alain Kalembu of the Democratic Republic of the Congo said the group had kept him in their prayers. Claire Holland of Jacksonville, Florida, said she felt very blessed to be there.

Attention is also on a planned November trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, which had been in doubt. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said on Friday that the pope may need to adjust his schedule according to his health. Leo's surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, told Vatican News he saw no clinical reasons why the trip should not go ahead. Latin Americans in the square welcomed that news.

Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro traded personal attacks in their first debate on Sunday, a week before the October 25 presidential run-off, Al Jazeera reported. The two called each other "liar" several times, accused each other of corruption and clashed over public security and healthcare.

Lula, 80, who is seeking a fourth term, called Bolsonaro "a habitual liar" and a "thug", and referred to him as a "militiaman", alluding to alleged ties to Rio de Janeiro's paramilitary groups. Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, called Lula a "clown" and raised a potential corruption case involving one of the president's sons. Lula pressed him on a corruption investigation involving his father, a question Bolsonaro dodged. Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence connected to efforts to overturn the 2022 election.

On policy, Bolsonaro focused on the cost of living and crime and accused Lula of "reckless spending" to get re-elected. Lula asked about Bolsonaro's plans to copy Argentine President Javier Milei's spending cuts; Bolsonaro avoided the question. On his father's COVID-19 handling, Bolsonaro said it was not an area of the best results and offered a "mea culpa".

Also on Sunday, federal police asked the Supreme Court to open an investigation into Bolsonaro over a money laundering accusation involving a lawyer close to him. He is already under investigation over links to banker Daniel Vorcaro.

Bolsonaro led the first round on October 4 with 47 percent to Lula's 45 percent, and polls suggest a close race with a slight Bolsonaro edge. Both campaigns want the 33 million voters who stayed home in round one. A second debate is scheduled for October 23.

Shawn Oliver, the Republican nominee for Massachusetts lieutenant governor, suspended his campaign on Sunday after being arrested following a rollover crash, Fox News reported. Oliver, 42, is also a New Bedford city councilor.

New Bedford police said officers responded around 11:40 p.m. Saturday to 448 Dartmouth St., where a vehicle had overturned after striking multiple parked vehicles. Five parked vehicles were involved, and two sustained extensive damage. Police identified Oliver as the driver and said he was taken to St. Luke's Hospital for treatment of injuries. After an investigation at the scene and the hospital, he was charged with operating under the influence of liquor, negligent operation, a marked lanes violation and speeding. The charges are allegations.

Republican gubernatorial nominee Mike Minogue, Oliver's running mate, called on him to step aside. "There is no excuse for driving under the influence," Minogue wrote on X, adding that Oliver was "lucky to be alive and lucky that no one innocent was hurt." Minogue said that if elected he would formally ask for Oliver's resignation. Oliver confirmed the suspension on X, saying "the election is too important to be overshadowed by personal matters." Minogue also criticised his Democratic opponent, Gov. Maura Healey, saying Massachusetts had not seen accountability from her; Fox's article did not include a response from her.

New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell, a Democrat, said the allegations were "deeply concerning" and that the public deserves to hear Oliver's explanation. The state Department of Correction, which employs Oliver, said he has been placed on restricted work duty while the circumstances are reviewed. The election is weeks away, with Minogue challenging Healey and Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll seeking another term.

A fire that swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday killed at least four service members and left 39 people in hospital, 19 of them in critical condition, the BBC reported. Prime Minister Mark Carney called it one of the worst peacetime tragedies on Canadian soil in the military's history.

The fire broke out around 4 p.m. local time. Major-General Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, said a grass fire ignited on a training range and "uncommonly strong winds caused it to spread rapidly and shift direction" toward soldiers taking part in exercises. He said the cause of the initial fire is under investigation. Local media had earlier reported that a gas main may have been struck during a live firing exercise, but the military later said investigators do not believe any explosions were caused by oil or gas infrastructure. The defence ministry said there are no indications of terrorist activity.

Officials identified the dead as Sgt Morgan Wong, Pte Shaun Farrell, Pte Aidan Goulding and Pte Hayden Lykkemark. They did not say whether they expect the toll to rise but said many people suffered severe burns. Carney described the fire as "violent" and "fast-moving" and said military and civilian crews fought it overnight in some of the worst conditions imaginable.

Edmonton's Royal Alexandra Hospital declared a code orange on Saturday evening and stood it down Sunday afternoon. Alberta's health service said the response lasted 10 hours and involved 22 ambulances and eight aircraft, and that ongoing care will be intensive. The base is about 120 miles from Edmonton, is one of the Canadian Army's busiest training bases, and can hold more than 1,000 people.

French President Emmanuel Macron called for "calm and order" in a national address on Sunday after protests on Saturday turned into rioting and looting, the BBC reported. Some disorder continued on a smaller scale in Paris and Lyon, where tear gas and stun grenades were fired, according to AFP.

About 550,000 people joined largely peaceful protests over fuel prices, the cost of living and declining public services. Macron distinguished between the protesters' "legitimate demands" and "those who destroyed, smashed and looted." France's interior ministry said about 2,400 people were arrested and about 1,000 police officers were injured, seven seriously. The BBC reported an estimated 1,500 shops and businesses were looted or destroyed, and rioters gutted the 19th-century city hall in Limoges.

Political reaction split along familiar lines. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez blamed "several thousand far-left individuals" and later "delinquents who looted." Jean-Luc Mélenchon of La France Insoumise said Nuñez and police chiefs had shown "complete incompetence." Marine Le Pen of the National Rally condemned the "exploitation" of anger by forces that encourage violence, and blamed the "Macronist administration". CGT union leader Sophie Binet said Macron failed to address students' concerns or the cost of living. The BBC said critics faulted the speech for lacking concrete detail, and the National Assembly's president, Yaël Braun-Pivet, wants an inquiry.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu holds a crisis cabinet meeting on Monday. Macron said prefects and mayors would draft measures to protect shops and civic buildings, and promised "full transparency" over the police response. Students begin a half-term break Monday, and unions and the gilets jaunes movement have announced large protests for November 5. A presidential election is due in April.

An Austrian Airlines flight from Tel Aviv to Vienna made an emergency landing in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Sunday night after a reported bomb threat, according to the BBC and Al Jazeera. The Bulgarian transport ministry said the Airbus A320, flight OS82, was near the Romanian border when the crew received the threat and chose to land in the Bulgarian capital.

Bulgaria's air force scrambled a MiG-29 fighter jet to escort the plane. The airline told AFP there were 51 passengers and six crew on board. The transport ministry said all had disembarked, and the BBC reported no injuries. Flight tracking data showed the plane left Ben Gurion Airport at 6:46 p.m. local time and landed at Vasil Levski airport at 9:43 p.m. Bulgarian time. Al Jazeera said ADS-B Exchange data showed the aircraft transmitting squawk code 7700, a general emergency signal.

Austrian Airlines confirmed a threat was made without giving details and said a security search was conducted. It said passengers would be rebooked onto other flights as quickly as possible once the search was complete. The Bulgarian ministry said a crisis response team was set up and authorities have opened an investigation. The BBC said it had sought comment from Lufthansa, Austrian Airlines' owner.

Both outlets noted a separate incident last month involving a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv. Authorities in the United Arab Emirates said the co-pilot, Hamam Al-Hammami, attacked the captain in a bid to crash the plane in Israel; he has been charged with terrorism offences in the UAE. The aircraft landed safely in Saudi Arabia, and Israel ordered identity checks on all pilots flying into the country.

Residents of Longyearbyen, a town in Norway's Svalbard archipelago, have been told they must no longer drink tap water because of heavy metal contamination that scientists have linked to thawing permafrost, the Guardian reports.

The town of 2,600 gets its main supply from Isdammen, a dammed lake about 2.5km long. Warmer temperatures have thawed permafrost, and newly exposed bedrock is leaching metals into the water. According to the Guardian, Longyearbyen is warming at between five and seven times the world average. Marjolaine Verret of the University Centre in Svalbard said the local shale bedrock contains pyrite, which oxidises on contact with water and oxygen and produces acid that can leach heavy metals.

The municipality first alerted residents in September last year, after manganese was found at 25 times the 50 micrograms per litre recommended by the Norwegian Institute of Public Health. Prolonged exposure to high manganese can cause neurological problems, particularly in children and infants. Temporary measures included a central tank of free purified water, filtered by the local brewery. Manganese has since dropped, but sulphate and nickel were found above recommended limits earlier this year, so the ban remains.

Mayor Terje Aunevik said manganese levels were "not dangerous" but that government guidelines had to be followed, and he acknowledged some residents were angry at the inconvenience. He has commissioned an investigation and said a completely new water mains supply may be needed. Options include filtration at Isdammen with a desalination plant as backup, or the reverse. He called either "extremely expensive" and technically challenging.

Verret said bedrock rich in pyrite and heavy metals, along with thawing permafrost, exists in other parts of the Arctic, so Longyearbyen could be a first example of such impacts, for instance in northern Canada and Alaska. Aunevik said other small communities should start thinking about what to do if it happens to their sources.

A Japanese-led space mission is set to launch on Monday in an attempt to collect a piece of Phobos, a moon of Mars, and bring it to Earth, the BBC reports. If it succeeds, it would be the first time a sample from Mars or its moons has been returned for laboratory analysis.

The Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft lifts off from the Tanegashima Space Center and is due to reach Phobos in August 2027. It will study Deimos, Mars's other moon, on arrival, then focus on Phobos. A small rover will scout a landing site, which is difficult because Phobos has little gravity of its own while sitting close to a planet with much stronger gravity, according to Prof Sara Russell of the Natural History Museum. The spacecraft will then land, use a robotic arm and two samplers, and send a capsule home in 2031, landing in South Australia. The sample will be only 10 grams, though Dr Chrysa Avdellidou said even individual grains allow useful science.

Scientists hope the material will settle how Mars's moons formed. One idea is that an impact threw debris off early Mars; the other is that they are captured asteroids. Russell said the two hypotheses would produce very distinct results. The sample may also contain grains of Mars knocked onto Phobos by impacts.

The BBC says NASA's Mars Sample Return mission has effectively been cancelled after Congress halted funding, while China plans its own Mars sampling mission, set to launch in 2028 and aiming to return material in 2031.

UK-listed companies issued 65 profit warnings in the three months to the end of September, the highest quarterly figure in two years, according to the consultancy EY-Parthenon, as the war in the Middle East pushes up business costs.

The figures come less than a fortnight before Chancellor John Healey's 28 October budget. Business leaders are pressing him for emergency support over fuel and energy costs. Healey has pledged "breathing space" for households and businesses but has warned the government has limited resources because the conflict has pushed borrowing costs to their highest in decades. The Sunday Times reported he plans to raise the threshold at which small firms start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, honouring a promise made by Andy Burnham.

EY-Parthenon said rising costs were the leading factor in 35% of warnings, and 38% specifically cited the Middle East conflict. Almost a fifth of UK-listed businesses have issued at least one warning in the past 12 months. Jo Robinson of EY-Parthenon said policy change and uncertainty were making forecasting and investment harder. Housebuilders have issued 14 warnings this year, above the 10 in 2008.

Separate Rightmove figures show asking prices for newly listed homes rose 1% in October to £371,015, but are down 0.1% over 12 months. Average two-year fixed mortgage rates have risen to 5.55% from 5.29% last month and 4.25% before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, adding about £250 to monthly payments on a new loan, according to the Guardian.
The Trades Union Congress has urged the chancellor to fund cost of living support through higher taxes on wealth and banks. A first-time buyer scheme pledged by Burnham is expected at the budget.

An alliance of Venezuelan opposition parties, the Unitary Democratic Platform, agreed at a meeting in Caracas on Sunday to "recognise and support the leadership of Maria Corina Machado", the exiled Nobel Peace Prize laureate, according to Al Jazeera.

The coalition renewed its demand for free elections and set out 14 proposals for a democratic transition, including freedom for political parties, release of all political prisoners and safe return for exiles. Former presidential candidate Edmundo Gonzalez backed the proposals, saying the will of Venezuelans must govern the nation. No date has been set for a new presidential vote. Delcy Rodriguez of the PSUV has been interim president since 3 January, after a US military operation to seize Nicolas Maduro.

Machado has lived in exile since leaving Venezuela last December to receive her Nobel Prize. Her party, Vente Venezuela, says authorities blocked her repeated attempts to return. She has told the Financial Times she wants elections by July next year. President Donald Trump has backed Rodriguez, and critics say he has been reluctant to press for elections, favouring a three-phase plan that starts with stabilisation and economic recovery. Al Jazeera reports that US officials, speaking anonymously to Reuters and Axios, expressed frustration at Machado's efforts to return; Axios quoted one calling it "political opportunism". Machado's response to that was not reported.

A third round of talks between the Rodriguez government and the opposition began this month, involving members of the 2015 National Assembly rather than Machado. The US State Department said the talks are producing "tangible reforms" and laying groundwork for credible elections.

The New South Wales government says it will introduce special legislation allowing the Mount Pleasant coal mine in the Hunter Valley to raise annual output by 4 million tonnes, to 16.5 million tonnes a year until 2032, according to the Guardian. The mine was the subject of High Court proceedings.

The announcement comes less than two weeks after the High Court ruled the approval of an expansion at the mine invalid. A majority found the Independent Planning Commission had not considered imposing conditions to minimise emissions from burning the coal overseas, known as scope 3 emissions, to the greatest extent possible. The company can currently mine up to 12.5 million tonnes under a separate modification approved in August.

Premier Chris Minns said 400 jobs would be lost before Christmas without intervention, and that MACH Energy had agreed to a jobs guarantee until 2032 if the bill passes. He said the bill would include restrictions on scope 3 emissions similar to those in the commission's approval of the Hunter Valley Operations extension. He said the government was "not seeking a full approval" and rejected the idea of a precedent for other mines. MACH Energy welcomed the plan and said the expansion had been through a rigorous assessment.

Critics disagree. Greens MP Sue Higginson said the bill bypasses the planning process and the High Court's ruling. Georgina Woods of the Lock the Gate Alliance said there was no threat to jobs because the mine already has approval to operate for six years. Elaine Johnson, the lawyer for the community group that brought the case, called the plan "legislative overreach". The bill is due in the next sitting fortnight.

Up to 20 of England's 155 consultant-led maternity units may have to close or change role to keep mothers and babies safe, Matthew Hopkins, the NHS Alliance's director for acute care, told the Guardian.

Hopkins said centralising childbirth services in fewer hospitals was "inevitable" and "the right thing", and urged ministers and MPs to show courage despite likely political backlash and longer journeys for some women. He said smaller units delivering 1,500 to 2,000 babies a year are increasingly unsustainable because of obstetrician shortages and a sharp rise in caesarean sections, and that many at-risk units are in rural or coastal areas. Caesarean births rose from 33% of births in England in 2020 to 45% last year. Hopkins also said hospital bosses fear a government maternity taskforce report, due before Christmas, will be tokenistic if it does not address the rise.

The comments drew objections. Hannah Leonard of the Royal College of Midwives said families rely on local units and care must remain close to home. Dr Alison Wright, president of the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, said there are safer solutions to workforce problems than closures. Liberal Democrat health spokesperson Helen Morgan said forcing women in labour to travel an hour or more is unsafe.

The Guardian notes that North Devon district hospital's unit in Barnstaple, shut temporarily in August over understaffing, is expected to have a reopening decision this week. About 194 women have given birth in Exeter, 43 miles away, because of the closure. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called such travel "not acceptable" at prime minister's questions.

The chief executive of Metinvest, one of Ukraine's biggest steel companies, has told the BBC the EU should drop import restrictions on Ukrainian steel, arguing Ukraine has been "bundled together" with measures aimed at cheap imports from countries such as China.

Yuriy Ryzhenkov called the new tariffs "unfair" and said they were introduced "without any consideration for the situation Ukraine is in". He wants "at least a carve out". The EU has capped tax-free steel imports at 18.3 million tonnes a year, a 47% reduction from 2024 levels, to protect member states' producers. Some country-specific quotas exist, and the BBC notes the EU-Ukraine free-trade agreement does not stop the bloc introducing separate trade protection measures. Ukraine's steel industry estimates exports to the EU could fall by 50 to 60%.

A European Commission spokesperson said the EU "took into account the difficult situation" of Ukraine. It said Ukraine's quota guarantees exports, though at a "level lower than in the past years", and that it had "offered compensations" to its largest suppliers.

Ryzhenkov said Russian strikes on Ukrainian steel mills had intensified, and that at one point in September no steel was produced in Ukraine for the first time in about 150 years. Almost 800 Metinvest workers have been killed since the war began. Before the 2022 invasion, metallurgy and mining made up roughly 10% of national income and a third of exports, and the EU is the top customer. Ryzhenkov said he expects this winter to be "one of the hardest in our history" and that Ukraine lacks logistics to reach other markets.

A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in the mass murder case against doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie and 29 followers, who are charged with murdering 191 children, the BBC reports. It is the first time Mackenzie faces a verdict on murder charges.

Prosecutors allege his cult forced children to starve so they could "meet Jesus". His teachings said education was forbidden and modern medicine "evil". Mackenzie and the others have pleaded not guilty and have repeatedly insisted nobody was forced to die. His former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but entered a plea deal and became a prosecution witness. Mackenzie and other leaders face further cases, including terrorism, radicalisation and denying children education.

Authorities said more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the coast, where Mackenzie moved followers after his main church shut in 2019. The first remains were found by herders in March 2023. Gravediggers told the BBC that each grave held at least three bodies, and some children had their hands and legs tied. Many bodies remain unidentified, and court papers refer to some as "unknown male child".

Stephen Mwiti said he lost all six of his children to the cult, and his former wife is among the accused. Peter Shukrani, rescued from the forest in March 2023, said his mother threw away his medicine. He described Mackenzie as his "spiritual father" and said nobody was forced to fast. The charge sheet is 298 pages long, and the BBC did not report the verdict date.

A US expedition to a remote Pacific atoll in search of evidence about Amelia Earhart has left without a find, saying an object it suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees, according to the Guardian.

"Unfortunately, we weren't able to find that smoking gun," said Steve Schultz of Purdue University on Nikumaroro, part of Kiribati and roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii. Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during an attempt to fly around the world at the equator. Nikumaroro is a leading candidate for where they may have crash-landed. Earlier visits found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s woman's shoe and a glass freckle cream jar attributed to Earhart.

The latest trip stemmed from 2020 satellite images showing an elongated white object in the shallows near the Taraia Peninsula. Other long-time Earhart researchers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew of the Archaeological Legacy Institute found aerial video showing what he suspected was a metallic glint. The 17-person team reached the atoll after a multi-day voyage and weather delays, and spent four days on research including metal detecting. They slept offshore, partly because of large coconut crabs.

Purdue said the "visual anomaly" was likely a collection of large trees deposited on the sandspit, and that the shine came from a carbonate coating, as with other items coated in concretized coral sand. The university, which helped fund Earhart's aircraft, called the result disappointing but a "new chapter" in the search. The Guardian notes it adds to a list of dismissed theories.
